summary: Specifies Metalink, an XML-based format that describes download locations (mirrors), cryptographic hashes and other information. Clients can use it to download files reliably. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a shopping list for a file that says where to get it, from which stores, and how to check you got the right one.

subtitle: An XML file that lists mirrors, hashes and signatures for a download so clients can fetch it reliably.

tldr.problem: A file is often available from many mirrors over FTP, HTTP and peer-to-peer, but a plain link or HTTP redirect points to one server and has no way to cope with a slow, stale or broken one.
tldr.mechanism: Metalink is an XML document that lists, for each file, its name, size, cryptographic hashes, optional signatures and a prioritized list of URLs and metadata URLs, so a client can verify the result and fall back to another source.
tldr.outcome: A client that reads a Metalink can switch mirrors, repair corrupted pieces and combine sources, while still checking everything against the listed hashes. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5854 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the Metalink 4 format and the application/metalink4+xml media type.

sections.title: Why Download Descriptions Are Needed
sections.content:
Identical copies of a file are often available in several places on the Internet, over protocols such as FTP, HTTP and peer-to-peer (P2P). Users are often shown a list of these mirror servers and must pick one by hand, based on location, priority or bandwidth.

Individual servers can be slow, outdated or unreachable, and that cannot be known until the download starts. Transmission errors can also corrupt the file, and there are no easy ways to repair it. A traditional HTTP redirect names only a single server, and HTTP has no provision for handling failures.

Metalink puts what is known about the mirrors, together with hashes and digital signatures, into one machine-readable file. A client can then fall back to another mirror, download chunks from several sources at once, and verify what it received, all without bothering the user.
sections.eli5: Imagine a toy you want is sold in many shops, but you only find out a shop is closed after you get there. A Metalink is a list of all the shops, so you can just try the next one.

sections.title: Metalink Documents
sections.content:
A Metalink Document describes a file or group of files, how to reach them, and metadata that identifies them. Its root element is metalink:metalink, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:metalink. Documents are serialized as XML 1.0 and identified by the media type application/metalink4+xml.

Documents MUST be well-formed XML, but the RFC defines no DTD, so they are not required to be valid in the XML sense. Documents that do not follow the specification are invalid and SHOULD NOT be used by processors. Whitespace around values is part of the content and MUST NOT be ignored, so values such as dates, integers and IRIs must not carry stray whitespace.

Addresses are IRIs (Internationalized Resource Identifiers). An IRI that is not also a URI MUST be mapped to a URI before it is dereferenced. Any element may carry an xml:lang attribute for its language. Dates use the RFC 3339 date-time form with an uppercase T and an uppercase Z when there is no numeric offset.
sections.eli5: A Metalink is a neatly labeled form written in a standard way, so any download program can read it the same way.

sections.title: Files, URLs and Pieces
sections.content:
The top-level element holds one or more metalink:file elements, plus optional generator, origin, published and updated elements. An origin SHOULD be present, and each of the others appears at most once.

Each file element stands for one unique file and MUST have a name attribute, the local file name to write. Names must be unique within the document. A name may include a relative directory path, but it MUST NOT begin with /, ./ or ../, contain /../, or end with /...

A file MUST contain at least one metalink:url or metalink:metaurl element. A url is an alternative place to download the same file. A metaurl points to a metadata file about it, such as a BitTorrent .torrent file or another Metalink Document. A file SHOULD have exactly one size, in octets, and a client MUST discard downloads whose length does not match.

Both url and metaurl take an optional priority from 1 to 999999. Lower values are used first, a missing priority counts as 999999, and several entries can share the same priority. A url may also have a location, a two-letter ISO 3166-1 country code for the server.

The metalink:pieces element lists hashes of contiguous, non-overlapping pieces of the file, in order, with a length attribute giving the piece size in octets. Every piece has that length except the last, which is the remainder and may be shorter.

The RFC assigns no meaning to the order of file, url or metaurl elements. Only the priority attribute ranks them.
sections.eli5: For each file the list says what to call it, how big it is, and where to find it. Lower numbers mean "try this shop first". For big files it can also give a checksum for each slice, so you can re-fetch just the broken slice.

sections.title: Descriptive Metadata and Hashes
sections.content:
Beyond locations, a file can carry human-readable metadata: identity (for Firefox 3.5 the identity would be "Firefox"), version ("3.5"), description, copyright, one or more language elements, os for the operating systems it suits, a logo, and a publisher with a name and optional URL. Publishers are RECOMMENDED to provide non-empty description, identity, version and publisher, but their absence is not an error and processors MUST NOT fail because of it.

The metalink:hash element holds a cryptographic hash in lowercase hexadecimal. A hash with a type attribute, such as sha-1 or sha-256, MUST cover the complete file. A hash inside a pieces element MUST NOT have a type and covers one piece, in file order. Type names come from the IANA registry "Hash Function Textual Names".

The metalink:signature element carries a digital signature of the file, with a required mediatype attribute; the RFC's example is an OpenPGP signature. Processor support for it is OPTIONAL. Processors MUST filter out invalid files obtained from url elements using the size and hashes.
sections.eli5: The list can also say what the file is called, which version it is, who made it and what language it is in. Each file gets a fingerprint, so you can tell if you got a fake or broken copy.

sections.title: Extending Metalink
sections.content:
Metalink allows foreign markup (elements from other XML vocabularies) almost anywhere in a document. A processor that meets foreign markup in a legal location MUST ignore it if it cannot process it, and MUST NOT stop or signal an error. Unknown foreign markup under metalink:file or metalink:metalink MAY be skipped and MUST NOT change the processor's behavior.

The Metalink namespace itself is reserved for future compatible revisions. Because software written for this version cannot tell new Metalink markup from an error, unrecognized markup in the Metalink namespace is treated as foreign markup too.

Extensions come in two kinds. A Simple Extension element has no attributes or child elements, only character data, and reads as a name/value property of its parent. A Structured Extension element must have at least one attribute or child element, and its meaning is defined by that extension's own specification.
sections.eli5: If someone adds a note to the list that your program does not understand, the program just skips it and carries on.

sections.title: Signatures, Spoofing and Weak Hashes
sections.content:
Metalink relies on existing XML security mechanisms. The root element or any file element MAY have an XML Signature (an enveloped signature). Signing and verifying are both OPTIONAL, but an implementation that supports either SHOULD implement RSA with a minimum key size of 2048 with SHA-256. Processors that verify signatures MUST reject documents whose signatures are invalid, MUST be able to verify RSA signatures, and MUST be able to use exclusive XML canonicalization. They MUST NOT reject a document merely because they cannot verify a signature it contains. Documents SHOULD NOT use MACs for signatures.

The RFC warns about spoofing: a malicious publisher can put false information anywhere in a Metalink, deceiving downloaders into fetching malicious or worthless content, or insert unrelated IRIs to aim a distributed denial-of-service attack. Digital signatures address this. Publishers are encouraged to serve Metalinks over HTTP under TLS and to include signatures of the files.

On hashes, some types in the IANA registry, including the whole Message Digest family, are considered insecure because of collisions. Generators and processors MUST support sha-256 and MAY support stronger hashes. A document that contains hashes SHOULD include sha-256 or stronger.
sections.eli5: A bad person could write a fake list that sends you to a harmful copy. Signing the list and using strong fingerprints lets your program notice the trick.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:metalink. It also registered the media type application/metalink4+xml with file extension .meta4, an optional charset parameter that behaves like that of application/xml, and the IESG as change controller. The registration names file transfer applications as the users of the type and says there are no known interoperability issues.
sections.eli5: The official name tags for the format were written down in a public list, so nobody else uses the same ones.
